# Continous Improvement of COMP 110

## Idea: Implement a series of "common errors/misconceptions" videos into the course.

Purpose: Students with very little coding experience may find COMP 110 difficult and may and may struggle with predictable, recurring misconceptions that slow their progress early in the semester.

## Summary of Analysis

My analysis explored the survey data collected amongst COMP 110 students. I filtered the dataset to isolate students who reported "None to less than one month" of programming experience and then examined their reported difficulty and understanding levels. Below is a bar plot visualization of the distribution of course difficulty ratings among low‑experience students.

<img src="/static/imgs/image1.png" alt="Bar Graph"  width="500"/>

The bar chart shows how students with low-experience cluster around the moderate to high difficulty levels (4-7) and very few report the course as easy. This means that less experienced coders face a moderate challange in taking this course. 

Next, I used a histogram to visualize the distribution of self-reported measures of understanding among low-experienced coders. The image below shows how many unexperienced programmers rated their understanding into the low to mid range (2-6), meaning that they had less understanding of the course as a whole.

<img src="/static/imgs/image2.png" alt="Histogram"  width="500"/>

Finally, I used a scatterplot, as shown below, to observe the relationship between difficuly and understanding. As I expected, there is an inverse relationship. This means that most students who reported high difficulty also reported lower understanding (and vice versa). This makes sense, as students who may have had a more challenging time in this course may also have less understanding of the course's material.

<img src="/static/imgs/image3.png" alt="Scatterplot"  width="500"/>

## Conclusions

Based on the data analysis and supporting visualizations, I believe that there is moderate support for idea of adding “common errors/misconceptions” videos to COMP 110. Low‑experience students  struggle more with debugging and understanding why their code fails. Even though the data does not directly measure the impact of videos, the patterns strongly suggest that targeted, short explanations of common mistakes could reduce confusion.
